Field surveys of Japanese grenadier anchovy in the Yangtze River estuary have provided robust estimates of its maximum body size. The largest individuals captured during a multi-year monitoring program reached a total length of 41 cm [Li = 41 cm], a value that likely represents the species' asymptotic size in this population. This measurement is derived from the upper limit of the length-frequency distribution, where few older individuals are encountered. In contrast, the size at which these fish first initiate reproductive activity is considerably smaller. Puberty, defined here as the onset of gonadal maturation, occurs at a total length of 25.5 cm [Lp = 25.5 cm], though some variation has been noted across different sampling years, with values ranging between 24 and 27 cm. This relatively large size at maturation relative to the ultimate length suggests a life-history strategy that prioritizes somatic growth before significant reproductive investment begins, a pattern common among iteroparous clupeiforms that undertake extensive spawning migrations.

The wet mass of newly hatched larvae of Coilia nasus is remarkably small. Based on measurements of freshly extruded ova, the average diameter of a fertilised egg is approximately 0.8 mm, which corresponds to an estimated wet weight at birth of 0.00027 g [Wwb = 0.00027 g]. This minute mass reflects the considerable yolk investment packaged within the transparent, pelagic egg. The yolk-sac larva that emerges following eclosion is entirely dependent on endogenous reserves for the first days of life, and its survival hinges on the timely onset of exogenous feeding. Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at 22 °C [T = 22 °C], the age at birth, defined as the point of chorion rupture, is approximately 7.75 days [ab = approximately 7.75 days]. It is noteworthy that active feeding commences shortly thereafter, with first prey capture typically observed around 6 days after hatching, indicating a very brief window of yolk dependence before the larva must successfully transition to an exotrophic mode of nutrition.

Adult body mass increases substantially as individuals approach their asymptotic length. The ultimate wet weight, corresponding to the 41 cm maximum total length, has been estimated at 221.3 grams [Wwi = 221.3 grams]. This value is derived from length-weight regressions that show a strong allometric relationship between length and mass in this species. In comparison, the wet weight at puberty, calculated for a fish of 25.5 cm total length, is considerably lower at 51.75 grams [Wwp = 51.75 grams]. This ten-fold difference in somatic mass between the onset of maturation and the maximum adult size underscores the extensive period of somatic growth that occurs after reproductive capability is first achieved. Such a pattern is typical of many pelagic schooling fishes, where early maturation allows for some reproductive contribution before the individual reaches the size that confers higher fecundity and competitive ability.

Reproductive output in Japanese grenadier anchovy has been quantified through examination of gravid females captured during the peak spawning season. At the prevailing water temperature of 17.5 °C [T = 17.5 °C], the maximum reproductive rate is expressed as a daily egg production of approximately 314 eggs per day [Ri = approximately 314 eggs per day]. This value is derived from direct counts of hydrated oocytes in females with fully developed ovaries, and it represents a peak rate attained by the largest, most fecund individuals. The annual reproductive effort is substantial, with multiple spawning events occurring over an extended breeding season. The measured rate reflects the species' high potential fecundity, a trait common to many small, pelagic, r-selected teleosts that experience high natural mortality. This daily output, when integrated over the entire spawning period, can result in tens of thousands of eggs being produced by a single female in a single year, ensuring that sufficient offspring enter the plankton to offset the high early life mortality characteristic of anadromous clupeiforms.

Longevity records for Coilia nasus indicate a maximum lifespan of 5 years [am = 5 years] under the thermal regime typical of the lower Yangtze River, where average annual water temperatures approximate 17.5 °C [T = 17.5 °C]. This lifespan is relatively modest for a fish of its size and contrasts with the longer lifespans observed in some other engraulid species from cooler, less seasonal environments. The age at birth of approximately 7.75 days [ab = approximately 7.75 days] at 22 °C [T = 22 °C] and the rapid early growth trajectory mean that individuals can reach the size at puberty of 25.5 cm total length within their first or second year of life. This combination of early maturation, high daily fecundity, and a relatively short reproductive lifespan results in a life-history strategy that depends heavily on high juvenile survival in favorable years to maintain population stability, rather than on iterated reproduction over many years. The adult body mass of 221.3 grams [Wwi = 221.3 grams] is typically achieved only in the oldest age classes, suggesting that the largest individuals contribute disproportionately to the population's overall egg production.
